items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: Because when I first heard Dizzy he was playing exactly like Roy Eldridge.

ctx.x: You worked from nine to four?

Nine to four in the morning. And then we’d go to a restaurant or someplace and get something to eat, and then they had places where trumpet players would go. All the trumpet players, we’d all end up there. As we used to call it we’d “cut each other” all night long. I stayed in there until one or two o’clock in the afternoon you know? But what a place to be to learn your instrument. Dizzy and all of us used to do that every morning. Charlie Shavers. We’d go someplace every morning, and play. And that is like a…

items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I didn’t feel like that I was in any way, shape, form up to playing with Roy Eldridge, you know, like eights or fours, something like that

ctx.x: Yes, we loved it. Because, there was no rehearsal. On the first night out, somebody would say in the dressing room, let’s play so and so and everybody would agree on it and then you go from there. And you play one fast tune, one medium tempo, then everybody would have a solo. Then you’d go to the piano player and tell him what key and what tune you wanted to play. And that would go on for ….let’s see, Coleman Hawkins, Roy Eldridge, Flip Phillips, Bill Harris. After that, have an intermission and Ella Fitzgerald.…

And then too, after that I got a band together in New York. I had Elvin Jones, Tommy Flanagan, Jimmy Forrest, and Joe Benjamin. I had a real good swinging band too, oh we were really doing it. I kept that band together for about six years.

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: the only two people I ever heard who could play endlessly were Pops and Roy Eldridge.

ctx.x: He came in an after hours bar one night because he used to carry his horn everywhere to play. I remember, he
almost made me want to quit. Oh, he could play. Oh, he had chops -- the only two people I ever heard who could play endlessly were Pops and Roy Eldridge.
